.\gemini\plugins\dotnet-diag\skills\dotnet-trace-collect\SKILL.md:83:3. For **long-running repros**: use PerfView with a `/StopOn` trigger that fires on the **symptom you want to capture** (e.g., `/StopOnPerfCounter`, `/StopOnGCEvent`, `/StopOnException`) and a circular buffer (`/CircularMB` + `/BufferSizeMB`). **Critical: the stop trigger must fire on the interesting event, not the recovery.** The circular buffer continuously overwrites old data, so if you trigger on recovery, the buffer may have already overwritten the interesting behavior by the time collection stops. Only add `/StartOn` if the start event is known to precede the stop event. For **slow requests**, do not include a stop trigger by default — let the user design one based on their specific scenario.

.\gemini\plugins\dotnet-diag\skills\clr-activation-debugging\SKILL.md:119:   - `V2.0 Capping is preventing consideration` — v4+ was skipped due to capping
.\gemini\plugins\dotnet-diag\skills\clr-activation-debugging\SKILL.md:156:- **`IsCapped`**: If 1, the shim's roll-forward semantics are capped at Whidbey (v2.0.50727) — it will NOT consider v4.0+ when enumerating installed runtimes. This is the mechanism that makes v4 installation non-impactful: legacy codepaths continue to behave as if v4 doesn't exist. On a v4-only machine with no .NET 3.5, a capped enumeration sees **no runtimes at all**. Capping does NOT prevent loading v4+ if a specific v4 version string is explicitly provided (e.g., via `CorBindToRuntimeEx("v4.0.30319", ...)` or via config with `useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy`).
.\gemini\plugins\dotnet-diag\skills\clr-activation-debugging\SKILL.md:169:- `UseLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy is set to {0|1}` — whether `<startup useLegacyV2RuntimeActivationPolicy="true">` is present. When 1, all runtimes are treated as candidates for legacy codepaths — meaning legacy shim APIs can enumerate and choose v4+. This can be used with multiple `<supportedRuntime>` entries, with other config options, or even with no `<supportedRuntime>` entries at all (in which case legacy APIs can simply enumerate v4). **Side effect:** turns off in-proc SxS with pre-v4 runtimes — locks them out of the process.
.\gemini\plugins\dotnet-diag\skills\clr-activation-debugging\SKILL.md:256:**Pattern:** `supportedRuntime` entries in config list multiple versions; the shim picks the first one that's installed. If v2.0 is listed first and .NET 3.5 is installed, v2.0 wins even though v4.0 is also available.

.\shared\skills\shadcn\SKILL.md:431:### `shadcn init` Breaks Geist Font in Next.js (Tailwind v4)
.\shared\skills\shadcn\SKILL.md:433:`shadcn init` rewrites `globals.css` and may introduce `--font-sans: var(--font-sans)` — a circular self-reference that breaks font loading. Tailwind v4's `@theme inline` resolves CSS custom properties at **parse time**, not runtime — so even `var(--font-geist-sans)` won't work because Next.js injects that variable via className at runtime.
.\shared\skills\shadcn\SKILL.md:446:--font-sans: var(--font-geist-sans);

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\SKILL.md:250:**Thermal bridge-free construction (ψ ≤ 0.01 W/mK):** Every junction, penetration, and transition must be designed to eliminate linear thermal bridges. The insulation envelope must be continuous without breaks. Window frames must overlap the insulation plane. Steel lintels must be thermally broken or replaced with insulated composite lintels. Foundation details must use insulated raft systems or thermal break elements.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\SKILL.md:254:**Mechanical Ventilation with Heat Recovery (MVHR):** With an airtight envelope, controlled ventilation is essential for indoor air quality. MVHR units recover ≥ 75% (PHI certification requires ≥ 75% effective heat recovery, many units achieve 85–95%) of the heat from outgoing exhaust air and transfer it to incoming fresh supply air. Supply air is delivered to living rooms and bedrooms; extract air is drawn from kitchens and bathrooms. Air change rate: 0.3–0.4 ACH (30 m³/h per person).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\SKILL.md:256:**Optimized solar gains with summer shading:** South-facing glazing (in the Northern Hemisphere) sized and positioned to maximize solar heat gain in winter while external shading (overhangs, brise-soleil, external blinds) prevents overheating in summer. A well-designed Passive House in a temperate climate derives 30–50% of its annual heating demand from passive solar gains through south glazing.

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:229:#### 12. Split-Level
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:235:- Half-level offsets create sightlines between adjacent spaces
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:239:**Programmatic Best-Fit:** Houses on sloping sites, small cultural buildings, retail (half-level browsing), libraries, schools
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:241:**Structural Implications:** Staggered floor slabs require careful structural coordination. Bearing walls at half-level offsets act as both gravity and lateral systems. Typical half-level: 1.5 m offset (for 3.0 m floor-to-floor). Foundation steps with the slope.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:244:- Villa Muller, Prague (Loos, 1930) — Raumplan: rooms at different levels within a cubic volume, each sized to its function (salon: high ceiling, bedroom: low ceiling)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:245:- Habitat 67, Montreal (Safdie, 1967) — 354 prefabricated boxes stacked in interlocking split-level configurations
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:277:**Setbacks:** Upper floors recessed from lower floors. Creates terraces, reduces perceived bulk, defines a streetwall at lower levels while allowing height above. Zoning-driven setback: New York 1916 Zoning (wedding cake massing). Design-driven setback: VIA 57 West (BIG, 2016).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:279:**Cantilevers:** Volumes projecting beyond the support structure below. Creates shelter at ground level, visual drama, and architectural assertion. Structural limit for RC: 3-6 m typical; for steel: 6-15 m; for post-tensioned: up to 20 m. Example: CCTV Headquarters (OMA, 2012) — 75 m cantilever at the top connecting two leaning towers.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:299:- **Podium sheltering:** A 2-4 story podium creates a wind-protected zone at ground level. Wind speed at pedestrian level behind a podium is 40-60% lower than at the exposed tower face.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:308:- Stagger floor plates to prevent upper floors from blocking lower-floor views
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:311:- Example: Absolute Towers, Mississauga (MAD, 2012) — each floor rotated 1-8 degrees to maximize views of Lake Ontario from every unit
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:315:**Datum:** Align key horizontal lines (cornice, string course, floor levels) with adjacent buildings. The streetwall datum creates visual continuity. Typical datum reference: adjacent cornice height (+/- 300 mm).

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:471:Every architectural concept begins with an abstract idea. The challenge is translating that idea into three-dimensional form. The following eight drivers provide distinct pathways from concept to architecture.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:481:**Risk:** Narrative can become literal or illustrative. The best narrative architecture communicates through spatial experience, not symbolism.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:487:**Process:** Select the primary material based on site context, budget, and desired atmospheric quality. Study its structural properties (compressive strength, tensile strength, modulus). Design the structural system to express those properties. Detail connections to reveal material behavior.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:489:**Example:** Therme Vals (Zumthor, 1996) — local Vals gneiss quartzite generates everything: wall thickness (600 mm composite: 2 layers of stone with insulated cavity), coursing rhythm (31/47/63 mm), bath temperatures etched into stone, even the light is filtered through stone edges.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:499:**Example:** Sendai Mediatheque (Ito, 2001) — 13 seaweed-like tube-columns of bundled steel pipes support 7 flat steel plates. Structure IS the architecture — there are no walls, no hidden frames, no false ceilings.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:501:**Risk:** Structural exhibitionism — complexity for its own sake. The best structural expression achieves elegance through economy.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:515:**Process:** Create a detailed program with areas (m2) for every space. Map adjacency requirements (must be adjacent, should be near, must be separated). Diagram circulation flows (public, staff, service, emergency). Translate the diagram into plan and section. The form is the program made spatial.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:531:**Process:** Define the target atmosphere in sensory terms (not formal terms). Specify: light quality (direct/diffuse, warm/cool, 2700K/4000K), acoustic character (reverberant/absorptive, RT60 target), material temperature (warm wood/cool stone), spatial proportion (compressive/expansive). Design every element to achieve that atmosphere.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:539:**Process:** Select the construction method (in-situ cast, precast, prefabricated, hand-laid, CNC-cut). Design the joint vocabulary (revealed/concealed, expressed/suppressed, same-material/contrasting). Detail the hierarchy of connections: primary (structure-to-structure), secondary (structure-to-envelope), tertiary (envelope-to-finish).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\SKILL.md:541:**Example:** Castelvecchio Museum renovation (Scarpa, 1973) — every joint between new (steel, concrete) and old (stone, brick, plaster) is a meticulously detailed micro-composition. Steel brackets are expressed, not hidden. Concrete meets stone with a deliberate gap. Each material retains its identity.

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:3:Comprehensive reference on 16 archetypal parti strategies for architectural design. Each entry documents the strategy's diagrammatic logic, historical lineage, structural implications, environmental characteristics, programmatic applications, scale range, and built examples.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:13:**Structural Implications:** Short spans perpendicular to the long axis (6-15 m). Load-bearing cross-walls at 3.6-7.5 m centers (residential) or frame structure at 6-9 m bays (commercial). Lateral stability from cross-walls, end cores, or braced bays every 20-40 m. Expansion joints every 40-60 m in RC. Foundations: continuous strip or pad footings.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:15:**Environmental Characteristics:** Optimal for cross-ventilation (building depth 12-15 m maximum for natural ventilation). South-facing facade (in northern hemisphere) receives maximum solar gain. North-facing facade provides even, glare-free daylight. Daylight penetration: 2-2.5x ceiling height from each facade. A 14 m deep bar with 3.0 m ceilings achieves daylight to the center.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:17:**Program Types Best Served:** Residential apartments (single-aspect: 6-8 m depth; dual-aspect: 12-15 m), school classroom wings (8-9 m depth), hospital wards (15-18 m depth with central corridor), laboratory buildings (service spine with labs on each side), linear galleries.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:30:**Diagrammatic Description:** Program arranged around one or more enclosed open-air spaces. The courtyard is a subtracted void — the negative space IS the design move. Rooms face inward toward the controlled microclimate of the courtyard.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:32:**Historical Lineage:** Among the oldest architectural strategies, found across all cultures: the Roman domus (atrium and peristyle), the Chinese siheyuan, the Islamic riad, the Spanish patio house. In modern architecture: Louis Kahn's Salk Institute (1965), Aldo van Eyck's Amsterdam Orphanage (1960), David Chipperfield's Am Kupfergraben 10 (2007).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:34:**Structural Implications:** Load-bearing perimeter walls or frame structure along all four sides. Corner conditions are critical: either column at corner, or cantilevered slabs from adjacent walls. Courtyard dimensions affect structural spans: 15-30 m courtyards allow economical RC framing; larger courtyards may need bridges or covered connections. Perimeter depth: 6-12 m (single-loaded) to 12-18 m (double-loaded).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:36:**Environmental Characteristics:** Courtyard microclimate varies with proportions. In hot-arid climates: narrow, deep courtyards (height:width 2:1 to 3:1) provide self-shading and cool air pooling at night. In temperate climates: wider courtyards (height:width 1:2 to 1:1) admit maximum winter sun. Courtyards reduce wind speed by 50-70% compared to exposed facades. Cross-ventilation from courtyard to exterior facade is highly effective.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:53:**Historical Lineage:** The Christian basilica established the cruciform as the default church plan (nave + transepts + chancel). Renaissance architects (Bramante, Michelangelo) developed the Greek cross (equal arms) for centralized churches. In secular architecture: Mies van der Rohe's cruciform columns, Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye ramp system, and OMA's Kunsthal, Rotterdam (1992).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:74:**Historical Lineage:** Mies van der Rohe's Brick Country House project (1924) established the pinwheel as a modern architectural strategy. The Barcelona Pavilion (1929) is its built apotheosis: walls slide past each other, never enclosing space completely. Gerrit Rietveld's Schroder House (1924) uses a pinwheel composition of colored planes. Frank Lloyd Wright's Usonian houses employ pinwheel plans radiating from a central masonry core.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:76:**Structural Implications:** No single load-bearing core at center — loads are distributed to perimeter walls and columns. Cantilevers at element terminations are essential for the visual effect of rotation (2-4 m typical). Roof planes may be independent (expressing each element's autonomy) or continuous (unifying the composition). Steel or timber frame is preferred for the slender profiles required.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:78:**Environmental Characteristics:** Each element can be oriented independently for optimal sun/wind/view response. The central void provides natural light and ventilation to the heart of the plan. Pinwheel plans typically have excellent cross-ventilation (multiple exposures per room). The open center prevents deep-plan conditions.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:95:**Historical Lineage:** The ancient Greek agora, the Roman forum, the medieval monastery, the Oxford/Cambridge college, and the American university campus. In modern architecture: Mies van der Rohe's IIT Campus (1940-58), Alvar Aalto's Saynatsalo Town Hall (1952), and Renzo Piano's Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre (1998).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:116:**Historical Lineage:** The medieval tower house, the campanile, the minaret, and the lighthouse are ancestral forms. The modern tower begins with the Chicago School (Home Insurance Building, Jenney, 1885) and matures with Mies (Lake Shore Drive, 1951), SOM (Lever House, 1952), and Fazlur Khan's structural innovations (tubular structures at SOM: John Hancock Center, 1969; Sears Tower, 1973).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:137:**Historical Lineage:** The podium-tower emerged from mid-20th century zoning codes that required street-level engagement with tower setbacks above. Lever House (SOM, 1952) pioneered the type. It became the default mixed-use urban form in Asian megacities (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bangkok).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:143:**Program Types Best Served:** Mixed-use urban development (retail podium + residential tower), hotels above convention centers, transit-oriented development (transit station at podium base), institutional (library/commons podium + office/residential tower).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:148:- Marina Bay Sands, Singapore (Safdie, 2010) — 3 towers (57 stories, 200 m) on a 5-story podium (casino, convention, retail, theater), connected by 340 m SkyPark at roof level
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:164:**Program Types Best Served:** Mixed-use urban complexes, transit hubs, mega-events (Olympic villages), incremental housing (infrastructure first, units added over time), disaster relief (rapid deployment of standardized units on permanent frame).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:170:- Nakagin Capsule Tower, Tokyo (Kurokawa, 1972) — 140 capsules (2.3 m x 3.8 m x 2.1 m) bolted to 2 interconnected concrete towers, designed for 25-year replacement cycle (never replaced; demolished 2022)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:177:**Diagrammatic Description:** A central or offset multi-story void surrounded by occupied floors on multiple levels. The atrium is the spatial and social heart — all movement, sightlines, and daylight converge on this void.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:181:**Structural Implications:** Long-span roof structure over atrium (trusses, space frames, cable-net, ETFE cushions). Floor plates span from perimeter to atrium edge — cantilevers or beams. Atrium glazing: structural glass walls (spider fittings on cable trusses) or framed curtain walls. Smoke management: minimum 2 m smoke reservoir at atrium top, mechanical smoke extract per BS 9999 or IBC Section 404.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:200:**Historical Lineage:** Ancient amphitheaters (Colosseum: 188 m x 156 m ellipse, 80 arched bays), medieval city walls, and 19th-century ring roads (Vienna Ringstrasse). In modern architecture: Alvar Aalto's Baker House at MIT (1949, serpentine bar as partial ring), Oscar Niemeyer's National Congress complex. Apple Park (Foster, 2017) is the definitive contemporary ring.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:202:**Structural Implications:** Curved structure: RC or steel frame following the ring geometry. For true circles: radial columns, ring beams, and circumferential floor plates. Construction efficiency depends on radius — large radii approximate straight segments. Expansion joints required at intervals (every 30-40 m of arc length). Foundation: continuous ring footing or piles.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:204:**Environmental Characteristics:** Central landscape is protected from wind and noise. The ring building itself acts as a sound and wind barrier. Solar exposure varies continuously around the ring — every orientation is present. Large rings (> 100 m diameter) enclose significant landscape (Apple Park: 12 hectares within the ring).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:221:**Historical Lineage:** The factory building (daylight sawtooth roofs), the department store (lightwells), the mid-century office (deep-plan with fluorescent lighting), and contemporary big-box retail and logistics. In architecture: the Sainsbury Centre (Foster, 1978) — 35 m wide clear-span shed; the Pompidou Centre (Piano + Rogers, 1977) — 48 m clear-span floors.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:240:**Diagrammatic Description:** A continuous low-rise (1-4 stories) fabric covering a large site area with high density. The mat building blurs the boundary between architecture and urbanism — it is simultaneously a building and a piece of city. Courtyards, light wells, streets, and plazas are woven into the mat.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:246:**Environmental Characteristics:** Excellent potential for natural ventilation and daylight via courtyards (every occupied space within 6-8 m of an external wall or courtyard). High thermal mass (concrete/masonry). Extensive green roofs possible (total roof area approximately equals site area). Low wind loads. Ground-coupled thermal performance.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:250:**Scale Range:** Minimum 5,000 m2 footprint to achieve mat character. Typical: 10,000-100,000 m2. Density: FAR 1.0-3.0 with 100% site coverage and 30-50% courtyard/void ratio.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:263:**Historical Lineage:** The Ponte Vecchio, Florence (1345) — shops spanning the Arno. The Bridge of Sighs, Venice (1600). Le Corbusier's Carpenter Center, Cambridge (1963) — ramp-as-bridge threading through the building. In contemporary architecture: CCTV Headquarters (OMA, 2012), The Bridge (Richard Rogers, 2004, Malpensa Airport).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:271:**Scale Range:** From a modest link bridge (3 m wide x 20 m span) to a mega-bridge (CCTV: 75 m cantilever/span at 162 m height). Most bridge-buildings span 20-60 m.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:274:- CCTV Headquarters, Beijing (OMA/Arup, 2012) — two leaning towers (234 m, 194 m) connected by a 75 m cantilever at the top and a 9-story base, continuous loop circulation, diagrid facade
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:276:- Carpenter Center, Cambridge (Le Corbusier, 1963) — ramp-as-bridge threads through the building connecting two streets at different levels, pilotis, brise-soleil, Le Corbusier's only building in North America
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:280:## 14. The Split-Section (Interlocking Half-Levels)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:284:**Historical Lineage:** Adolf Loos's Raumplan (Villa Muller, Prague, 1930) is the seminal precedent — each room at a different level, sized in height to its function. Le Corbusier's duplex units in the Unite d'Habitation use a split-section to create double-height living spaces with single-height bedrooms, accessed by a skip-stop corridor.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:286:**Structural Implications:** Staggered floor slabs require bearing walls or columns at half-level offsets. Short spans (3-6 m) between bearing walls. Slabs at different levels create inherent lateral bracing. Foundation steps with the natural grade on sloping sites, reducing cut-and-fill. Structure is more complex to build than flat-slab construction — requires skilled formwork or precast panels.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:288:**Environmental Characteristics:** Half-level offsets allow sightlines between spaces, creating visual openness without full double-height volumes. Natural ventilation benefits from section height variation (warm air rises to upper levels and is exhausted; cool air enters at lower levels). Daylight can penetrate deeper via level changes. Energy-efficient: no wasted volume — each space is exactly as tall as needed.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:290:**Program Types Best Served:** Houses on slopes, duplexes and maisonettes, libraries (reading levels at half-stories), retail (browsing levels), small cultural buildings, hillside housing.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:295:- Villa Muller, Prague (Loos, 1930) — cubic exterior conceals 10+ distinct levels within, each room at a height appropriate to its function (salon: 3.6 m, bedroom: 2.7 m, study: 2.4 m)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:296:- Unite d'Habitation, Marseille (Le Corbusier, 1952) — skip-stop corridor at every third floor, duplex apartments with double-height living rooms (4.8 m) and single-height bedrooms (2.3 m), corridor: 2.6 m wide x 2.3 m high
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:297:- Gifu Kitagata Apartment Building (SANAA, 1998) — 10-story, 107 units, split-level sections creating terraces and double-height spaces within a repetitive structural grid
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:339:- Linked Hybrid, Beijing (Holl, 2009) — 8 towers with stacked programs: commercial podium, residential floors, sky-bridge amenities (pool, gym, gallery) at floors 12-18; each tower has a distinct color/material identity at different levels
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:377:When choosing between competing parti types for a specific project, evaluate each against these seven criteria:
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:387:5. **Circulation efficiency:** What is the net-to-gross ratio? Simple bars achieve 82-88% (residential); complex partis (radial, spiral) may drop to 65-72%.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\parti-strategies.md:397:**Beaux-Arts Tradition (1800s-1930s):** The parti was the "big idea" — the axial diagram that governed the entire composition. Students at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts competed in esquisse (sketch) competitions where the parti was established in a single 12-hour session and could not be changed. The parti was understood as a plan composition — typically symmetrical, axial, and hierarchical. Jean-Nicolas-Louis Durand's "Precis des lecons" (1802-1805) codified building types as combinatoric plans: grids, crosses, courtyards, rotundas.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:16:**Airtightness strategy:** Wet-plastered dense blockwork inner leaf provides the airtight layer. All joints between block and floor slab, block and window reveal, block and roof plate must be parged or taped with compatible sealant. Service penetrations sealed with proprietary grommets.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:44:- Steel studs (90–150 mm at 600 centres) with mineral wool fill (NB: steel studs are severe thermal bridges — the external insulation must dominate)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:51:**Critical note:** Steel studs have λ ≈ 50 W/mK (vs. timber at 0.13 or insulation at 0.035). Without continuous external insulation, the effective U-value can be 2–3× the clear-wall value. A 100 mm steel stud wall insulated only between studs achieves an effective U-value of approximately 0.5 W/m²K — nowhere near Passive House. The external wrap of continuous insulation is mandatory.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:82:### 2.2 Cold Roof (Insulation at Ceiling Level)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:87:- Airtight membrane at ceiling level (connected to wall airtight layer at eaves)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:94:### 2.3 Rafter-Level Insulation (Vaulted Ceiling)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:122:**Airtightness:** The concrete slab is the airtight layer at floor level. The DPM beneath the slab is the moisture barrier. The junction between the slab/DPM and the wall airtight layer must be continuous — typically achieved by lapping the DPM to the wall membrane with compatible tape.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:167:- Aluminium (thermally broken): Uf 1.2–2.0 W/m²K. Difficult to achieve Passive House targets without very wide thermal breaks (≥40 mm). Some PHI-certified systems exist (e.g., Schuco AWS 90.SI+, Reynaers Hi-Finity).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:170:**Installation position:** The window frame must be positioned within the insulation zone — typically at the outer face of the structural wall, overlapped by ≥40 mm of external insulation. This minimizes the installation thermal bridge (ψ_install). Setting the window at the inner face of the wall creates a severe thermal bridge.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:179:External doors must achieve Ud ≤ 0.80 W/m²K and airtight seals on all four edges (typically triple-seal compression gaskets). Threshold details are critical: the threshold must be thermally broken and insulated beneath.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:208:| ProClima Intello Plus | Intelligent VCL | 0.25–10 m (variable) | Most widely used in Passive House. Variable vapour resistance: low Sd in summer (allows inward drying), high Sd in winter (prevents interstitial condensation). |
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:222:| ProClima Kaflex | Pipe/cable penetrations through membrane | Grommeted sleeve for individual penetrations. |
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:228:1. **Planning:** Draw the airtight layer on every building section and plan drawing before construction begins. Identify every junction, penetration, and transition.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:256:- Sound pressure level ≤ 25 dB(A) at 1 m from any supply/extract terminal in habitable rooms
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:262:- Balance: total supply ≈ total extract (slight negative pressure acceptable to prevent moisture migration into structure)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:294:2. Adjust dampers to achieve design airflow rates at each terminal (±10% tolerance)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:306:### 7.1 Prevention Strategies
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:327:### 7.2 Active Cooling (When Prevention Is Insufficient)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:329:In hot climates, hot-humid climates, or urban heat island conditions, passive strategies alone may not prevent overheating. The Passive House standard allows active cooling with a cooling demand limit of ≤ 15 kWh/m²a (plus dehumidification allowance in humid climates).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:345:4. **Thermal bridges:** Calculate linear thermal transmittance (ψ-value) for every junction using 2D thermal simulation (THERM, Flixo, HTFlux) or approved catalogue values. Input length × ψ for each bridge type.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:346:5. **Windows:** Input window dimensions, frame U-value (Uf), glazing U-value (Ug), spacer ψ-value, installation ψ-value, g-value, frame percentage, shading factors (overhang, reveal, winter shading), and orientation.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:394:- **Significance:** BREEAM Outstanding and Passive House certified. Thatched facade (locally sourced Norfolk reed — a bio-based cladding material with near-zero embodied carbon). Demonstrates that Passive House and BREEAM can be achieved simultaneously with innovative natural materials.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:398:- **Significance:** Demonstrates Passive House in a Korean climate with extreme seasonal variation (−15°C winter to +35°C summer with 90% humidity). .\shared\skills\skills-architects\building-sustainability\references\passive-house.md:443:- **Indoor air quality:** Continuous filtered fresh air via MVHR. CO2 levels consistently below 1000 ppm. Reduced allergens and pollutants. Beneficial for asthma and allergy sufferers.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:11:The solar envelope, developed by Ralph Knowles at USC beginning in the 1970s and published in "Energy and Form" (1974) and "Sun Rhythm Form" (1981), defines the maximum buildable volume on a site that will not cast shadows on adjacent properties beyond specified time limits.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:38:| 35-50 deg (temperate) | Significant south-slope; north face severely constrained | Low-rise north, mid-rise south, 2-5 stories |
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:46:- Dense urban blocks can still achieve significant height by concentrating mass on the south side of the block
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:47:- Knowles demonstrated that solar envelope development can achieve 80-90% of the density of conventional zoning while guaranteeing solar access to all units
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:55:The Lawson Comfort Criteria (after T.V. Lawson, University of Bristol, 1975/2001) define acceptable wind speeds for different pedestrian activities. These criteria are the standard for wind microclimate assessment in the UK, Europe, and much of Asia.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:67:**Downwash:** Wind hitting a tall building's windward face is deflected downward, accelerating at ground level. A 100 m tower can create ground-level wind speeds 2-3x the ambient wind at 10 m height. Mitigation: podium base (3-6 stories) breaks the downwash before it reaches ground level. Canopies at 3-5 m above grade provide shelter.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:71:**Channeling:** Parallel buildings (street canyons) can channel and accelerate wind. Narrow gaps between buildings (< 0.5x building height) create high-velocity jets. Mitigation: stagger buildings to prevent continuous channels, provide windbreaks (planting, screens, colonnades).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:77:1. **Podium + tower:** Podium (3-6 stories) intercepts downwash. Tower setback > 5 m from podium edge. Ground-level wind speed reduced by 40-60% compared to tower without podium.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:79:3. **Porous base:** Colonnade or arcade at ground level (3-4 m high, 3-6 m deep) provides pedestrian shelter while allowing wind to pass through, reducing pressure buildup.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:87:- **Pedestrian-Level Assessment:** Combine wind data (meteorological records, minimum 10 years hourly data) with CFD/wind tunnel results. Report wind speed and frequency at each key location (entrances, seating, crossings) against Lawson criteria.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:95:View corridor analysis ensures that new development preserves or enhances significant public views to landmarks, waterfronts, mountains, or skylines.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:98:- Consult the local development plan for designated view corridors (London View Management Framework identifies 27 protected views; San Francisco's Urban Design Guidelines identify 17)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:104:- Define the vertical extent: ground level to sky (or to a specific landmark elevation)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:117:- **Twisting:** Rotate the building plan at upper floors to align with view corridors. Each floor plate is rotated 1-3 degrees to prevent view obstruction and capture oblique views (Absolute Towers, Mississauga).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:126:Shadow impact assessment determines whether new development will unacceptably reduce solar access to neighboring properties, public spaces, or solar installations.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:129:- **UK (BRE Guide, 2011):** Existing windows should receive at least 25% of the annual probable sunlight hours (APSH), including 5% during winter (September 21 to March 21). If the proposed development reduces APSH by more than 20% of its existing value, the loss is noticeable.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:137:2. **Model proposed development:** Insert proposed massing into the 3D context model
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:141:   - Summer solstice (June 21 NH / December 21 SH) — longest shadows in morning/evening
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:187:**Tower Taper:** Reduction in floor plate area at upper levels. Improves sky view factor at ground level, reduces wind loads, and creates a more elegant silhouette. Common approach: 10-20% reduction in floor area over the top 1/3 of the building.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:198:- Higher FAR = more floor area = more revenue (in market-driven contexts)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:206:3. **Use transfer structures:** Where podium grids differ from tower grids, transfer structures allow each zone to use its optimal column spacing — maximizing usable area at each level.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:234:- **Stagger buildings in plan** to prevent upwind buildings from blocking breezes to downwind buildings. Stagger by at least 50% of building width.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:239:- **Wind catchers (Badgir/Malqaf):** Towers projecting above the roof to capture wind at higher velocities and direct it downward into the building. Traditional in Middle Eastern and South Asian architecture (minimum 3-5 m above roof level).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:241:- **Sky courts and terraces:** Open-air voids cut into the building mass to introduce fresh air at intermediate levels. Effective in tropical climates where continuous floor plates would trap heat. Example: WOHA's Parkroyal on Pickering, Singapore (2013) — sky gardens every 4-5 floors.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:242:- **Double-skin facades with ventilated cavity:** 600-1,200 mm cavity between inner and outer skins. Buoyancy-driven airflow in the cavity removes solar heat gain. Inner skin can have operable windows for user-controlled ventilation even in high-rise buildings.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:252:**Massing Strategy:** Aerodynamic circular plan tapering at base and top. Maximum diameter: 56.5 m at level 17; minimum: 49 m at base and 26 m at top. The bulging profile directs wind around the building, reducing ground-level wind speeds by 50% compared to a rectangular tower of equivalent height. Six helical lightwells (each 6 stories high) spiral around the perimeter, providing natural ventilation and daylight to the deep plan. Diagrid structure (triangulated steel frame) eliminates the need for internal columns, creating 15 m clear spans from core to perimeter. The structure uses 21% less steel than a conventional rectangular frame of equivalent floor area.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:258:**Massing Strategy:** Figure-eight plan form creates two courtyards. The cross-section ramps continuously from ground-level commercial at the south to penthouse apartments at the top of the north arm. Every apartment has a private outdoor terrace. The ramping section creates a continuous path from ground to 10th floor — residents can cycle from street to their front door. The south arm is low (3-4 stories) to admit maximum winter sun to the north courtyard. The north arm rises to 10 stories, capturing views over the landscape. Massing directly expresses the program gradient: commercial (ground), townhouses (lower levels), apartments (middle), penthouses (top).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:266:### Case Study 4: Linked Hybrid (Steven Holl, 2009)
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:270:**Massing Strategy:** Eight towers of varying height (14-22 stories) connected at floors 12-18 by a loop of sky bridges containing public amenities (pool, gym, cafe, gallery, theater). The ring of bridges creates a "city within a city" — a raised public realm accessed from any tower. Below the bridges, each tower has a distinct residential character. Ground level is a continuous public landscape with retail, educational, and cultural uses. The massing uses a "porous" model: spaces between towers allow wind, light, and view to penetrate. Ground-source geothermal system (660 wells, 100 m deep) provides all heating and cooling.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:276:**Massing Strategy:** Staggered balconies of varying depth (3.0-3.35 m) support 900 trees, 5,000 shrubs, and 11,000 perennial plants — the biomass equivalent of 20,000 m2 of forest. The vegetation performs multiple massing functions: shading (trees block summer sun at high altitude while admitting winter sun when deciduous), wind buffering (plant mass reduces wind speed at balcony level by 30-50%), air filtration (20 tonnes of CO2 absorbed per year), and biodiversity (1,600 bird and butterfly specimens observed). The building mass is articulated as a stack of thick inhabited terraces rather than a smooth glass tower. Structural reinforcement for plant loads: 1.3 tonnes per tree including soil, irrigation, and wind load on mature canopy. Irrigation system draws from building greywater.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:282:**Massing Strategy:** A "vertical village" organized as a sandwich: community plaza and hawker center at ground level (public), medical center and community facilities in the middle (semi-public), residential apartments for seniors at the top (private), with a 900 m2 community farm on the roof. The massing creates a "layered cake" of public-to-private uses, with the most public functions at grade and the most private at the top. A central void (community living room) connects all levels visually and provides daylight and ventilation. Lush tropical planting covers every facade and terrace — green plot ratio of 112%. The compact massing achieves very high density (FAR 3.64) on a tiny urban site while maintaining a village-like social character.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:288:**Massing Strategy:** Instead of the typical Singapore tower-on-podium typology, OMA stacked 31 six-story apartment blocks (each 70 m long) in a hexagonal arrangement, rotated 60 degrees at each level. The stacking creates communal sky gardens and courtyards at every intersection. The resulting mass is 24 stories at its highest but reads as a low-rise village in the sky. Every apartment has cross-ventilation (maximum 12 m depth). 60% of the site is open landscape. The interlocking mass provides self-shading in Singapore's equatorial climate. Structural system: conventional RC frames for each block, with massive transfer structures at block intersections (post-tensioned concrete transfer plates, 1.2 m thick).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:306:**Massing Strategy:** Dense, low-rise courtyard fabric reinterpreting the traditional Arabic medina. Buildings are clustered tightly to create narrow shaded streets (3-6 m wide, 15-20 m tall walls = height-to-width ratio of 3:1 to 6:1). This produces self-shading: 70% of outdoor surfaces are in shade at midday. Wind towers (modern interpretation of traditional badgir) rise 20 m above the roofline, capturing prevailing breezes and directing them down into the streets — reducing ambient temperature by 15-20 C at pedestrian level compared to exposed conditions. The entire campus is raised on a 7 m podium to separate pedestrian realm from service/logistics below. Photovoltaic canopies shade the rooftop. GRC (glass-reinforced concrete) cladding panels with parametrically optimized mashrabiya patterns filter light while preventing direct solar gain. 54% energy reduction compared to Abu Dhabi baseline.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:312:**Massing Strategy:** Hybrid of European courtyard block and Manhattan tower — BIG termed it the "courtscraper." The massing rises from a single story at the north (preserving neighbor's light and views) to 32 stories at the south-west corner (maximizing the building's own Hudson River views). The resulting tetrahedron-like form encloses a 2,000 m2 landscaped courtyard at its center. The sloping west facade creates a hyperbolic paraboloid geometry — each floor plate is a slightly different shape, but all are derived from the same parametric logic. Despite the complex exterior geometry, the structural system is a conventional flat-plate RC frame with slightly varying column positions per floor. FAR achieved: 10.8. Every apartment has Hudson River views, which would be impossible with a conventional rectangular tower on this site.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\concept-design\references\massing-methods.md:318:**Massing Strategy:** Four sky gardens (each 4 stories tall) are inserted into the tower mass at regular intervals, creating a "hotel-in-a-garden" effect. The podium is a continuous landscape — contoured green terraces flowing over the building base like topography. Total green area is 15,000 m2 — double the site area, achieving a green plot ratio of 200%. The sky gardens provide natural ventilation to adjacent hotel corridors, reducing mechanical cooling loads by 30%. Solar collectors on the rooftop and facade-integrated planters shade 60% of the building's glazed surface. Rainwater harvested from the extensive planted surfaces irrigates the gardens via gravity-fed drip system, reducing potable water consumption for irrigation by 100%. Structural system: conventional RC frame with post-tensioned transfer beams at sky garden levels (1.8 m deep) to support the 4-story planted terraces above.

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\country-japan\SKILL.md:174:### 3.1 Two-Level Seismic Design
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\country-japan\SKILL.md:177:- **Level 1 (Damage Limit)** -- frequent earthquakes (~50-year return) -- building remains undamaged, structurally elastic. Design seismic shear coefficient C0 = 0.2 (multiplier on weight).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\country-japan\SKILL.md:178:- **Level 2 (Life Safety / Ultimate)** -- rare earthquakes (~475-year return, possibly 2475-year for important structures) -- building may sustain damage but no collapse. Design shear coefficient C0 = 1.0.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\country-japan\SKILL.md:180:The 1981 revision (Shintaishin -- "New Earthquake-Resistance Standard") introduced this two-level approach. Buildings built before 1981 are designated "Kyu-taishin" and many have been retrofitted.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\country-japan\SKILL.md:184:- **General buildings**: design per Level 1 + Level 2 capacity
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\country-japan\SKILL.md:212:- **Building Standards Act** -- "preventive fire-resistance" (Yobo Bosai) -- structural compartmentation, fire-resistance, smoke control DESIGN

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:15:Roman architect-engineer who authored *De Architectura* (c. 30 BC), the only surviving architectural treatise from antiquity. Established the foundational triad of *firmitas* (structural soundness), *utilitas* (functional fitness), and *venustas* (beauty through proportion). His system of proportional orders (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian) codified column ratios, intercolumniation, and entasis into reproducible rules. Apply Vitruvian thinking when establishing first-principles performance criteria for any project -- the triad remains the most durable evaluation framework in architecture.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:18:Humanist polymath whose *De Re Aedificatoria* (1452) reinterpreted Vitruvius for the Renaissance, arguing that beauty arises from *concinnitas* -- the harmonious integration of parts such that nothing can be added or removed without diminishment. Pioneered the idea of the architect as intellectual author rather than master mason. His facade for Santa Maria Novella (Florence) demonstrated proportional ratios derived from musical harmony. Use Alberti's framework when designing facades or ensembles where part-to-whole mathematical relationships must read clearly.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:21:Goldsmith-turned-architect who solved the unsolvable: spanning the 42m octagonal drum of Florence Cathedral (1420-1436) without centering, using a double-shell herringbone brick technique with self-supporting rings. Invented linear perspective as a design and representational tool. His Ospedale degli Innocenti (1419) established the Renaissance arcade module. Apply Brunelleschi's thinking when confronting structural problems that require invention beyond standard engineering practice, and when modular repetition must generate civic dignity.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:24:His *Quattro Libri dell'Architettura* (1570) became the most influential architectural treatise ever published, disseminating systematic proportional rules, room-ratio hierarchies (1:1, 2:3, 1:2), and the temple-front motif for domestic architecture. Villa Rotonda (c. 1567) achieved perfect four-fold symmetry on a hilltop with identical porticos on each facade. San Giorgio Maggiore (Venice) resolved the classical temple front against a basilican section. His villa typology -- elevated piano nobile, projecting portico, symmetrical wings, landscape axis -- was exported globally through pattern books, shaping Georgian England, Jeffersonian America, and colonial architecture worldwide. Palladian principles apply whenever a project requires proportional rigor, axial clarity, and the translation of monumental language into residential or civic scale.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:34:Designer, writer, and socialist activist who founded the Arts and Crafts movement by insisting on the unity of art and labor. Red House (1859, with Philip Webb) rejected Victorian eclecticism for honest brick, functional plan, and integrated decorative arts. Morris & Co. produced wallpapers, textiles, furniture, and stained glass as a total design enterprise. His dictum "Have nothing in your houses that you do not know to be useful or believe to be beautiful" links ethics to aesthetics. Apply Morris when a project demands material honesty, craft-based detailing, and social purpose embedded in design decisions.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:40:Catalan architect who developed an entirely original structural-ornamental language through catenary arch experiments (hanging chain models inverted to find pure compression forms), ruled-surface geometries (hyperboloid, helicoid, conoid), and *trencadis* (broken-tile mosaic). Sagrada Familia (begun 1882, ongoing) synthesizes branching-column structural trees with hyperbolic paraboloid vaults. Casa Batllo and Casa Mila demonstrate organic facades as structural surfaces. Park Guell integrates landscape and architecture through continuous vaulted infrastructure. Apply Gaudi when complex curvature must be structurally rational, or when ornament and structure should be inseparable.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:47:Chicago School pioneer who articulated "form follows function" (1896 essay "The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered") not as stripped austerity but as organic expression -- ornament should emerge from the building's purpose like leaves from a stem. The Guaranty Building (Buffalo, 1895) established the tripartite tall building expression (base-shaft-capital) with terra-cotta ornament encoding structural logic. Wainwright Building (St. Louis, 1891) achieved vertical emphasis through recessed spandrels. Apply Sullivan when a tall or repetitive structure needs expressive articulation that reveals rather than conceals its organizational logic.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:50:Polemicist whose *Ornament and Crime* (1908/1913) attacked applied decoration as culturally regressive, yet his architecture was richly spatial and materially luxurious. Invented the *Raumplan* -- a three-dimensional plan where rooms at different ceiling heights interlock within a single volume, with stairs connecting half-levels. Villa Muller (Prague, 1930) is the masterwork: a plain stucco exterior concealing an interior of marble, onyx, and mahogany in continuously shifting spatial sequences. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:53:French architect who elevated reinforced concrete from engineering material to architectural medium. The apartment building at 25 bis Rue Franklin (Paris, 1903) exposed the concrete frame on the facade, filling panels with floral ceramic tile. His reconstruction of Le Havre (1945-1964) applied classical urbanism through a concrete structural module. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:56:The most prolific and influential American architect, whose 70-year career produced over 500 built works across every scale. Fallingwater (1939) cantilevered reinforced concrete terraces over a waterfall, fusing building and landscape in the most celebrated house of the 20th century. The Johnson Wax Headquarters (1939) used dendriform columns (lily-pad mushroom columns) to create a luminous top-lit workspace. The Guggenheim Museum (NYC, 1959) inverted the museum typology into a continuous spiral ramp around a top-lit atrium. His *Usonian* houses (1930s-1950s) proposed affordable, L-plan, slab-on-grade residences with radiant-heated concrete floors, carports, and open kitchens -- prefiguring postwar suburban living. His concept of *organic architecture* -- buildings growing from site, program, and materials as naturally as a plant from its seed -- remains the most potent alternative to rationalist modernism. Apply Wright when a project demands radical site integration, flowing interior space, and formal innovation rooted in natural process.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:69:Founded the Bauhaus (Weimar, 1919; Dessau, 1925) on the principle that all design disciplines -- architecture, furniture, graphics, textiles, theater -- should be taught and practiced as a unified whole. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:75:The most influential architect of the 20th century, whose career spanned from Purist painting to urban planning at continental scale. *Vers une Architecture* (1923) demanded architecture engage the machine age. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:78:Austrian-born, Los Angeles-based architect who developed *biorealism* -- architecture calibrated to human nervous-system response through transparency, cross-ventilation, connection to landscape, and precise material junctions. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:304:**Legacy:** Birthed the modern design studio, influenced the Bauhaus (despite opposing conclusions about industry), established the ethical framework linking design quality to social justice, and produced a domestic architecture language of warmth and material authenticity that remains influential.

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:316:**Characteristics:** Celebration of speed, technology, and industrial dynamism; diagonal and oblique forms suggesting motion; stepped-back profiles with external elevators and sky-bridges; integration of transportation infrastructure with architecture; rejection of all historical reference; materials of the machine age (steel, glass, concrete); expendability (buildings as temporary, replaceable); aerodynamic profiles and streamlined surfaces.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:317:**Design principles:** "We must invent and rebuild the Futurist city like an immense tumultuous shipyard, agile, mobile and dynamic in every detail" (Sant'Elia). .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:327:**Legacy:** De Stijl provided the formal vocabulary for the open plan and free facade, directly influencing Mies van der Rohe's Barcelona Pavilion and subsequent International Style architecture. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:335:**Legacy:** Constructivism produced some of the most radical architectural propositions of any era. Its influence on the Bauhaus, on Rem Koolhaas (who studied the movement extensively in his book *Delirious New York* and subsequent research), and on contemporary parametric and social-infrastructure architecture remains profound. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:340:**Characteristics:** Unity of art, craft, and technology in education and practice; preliminary course (*Vorkurs*) exploring material properties; workshop-based learning (metal, weaving, carpentry, typography, theater); industrial prototyping; standardized components; flat roofs, white walls, steel-and-glass curtain walls, asymmetric massing; furniture design (Breuer's Wassily Chair, tubular steel) as architecture at small scale.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:342:**Design principles:** Three phases reflecting three directors: Gropius (1919-1928) emphasized craft-industry synthesis and collaborative pedagogy; Hannes Meyer (1928-1930) pushed radical functionalism, collective design, and social analysis ("building is a biological process, not an aesthetic one"); Mies van der Rohe (1930-1933) reduced the curriculum to pure architecture and material precision. The *Vorkurs* (preliminary course) taught by Itten, then Moholy-Nagy, then Albers, trained perception through material experiments, color theory, and three-dimensional composition -- a pedagogical model still foundational to design education worldwide.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:343:**Canonical domestic artifacts:** Breuer's Wassily Chair (1925, tubular steel), Breuer's Cesca Chair (1928, cantilevered), Gropius's Bauhaus typography, Anni Albers's woven textiles, Marianne Brandt's metalwork (teapot, ashtray, desk lamp).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:344:**Legacy:** The Bauhaus is the single most influential design school in history. Its pedagogical model (foundation course, workshop integration, industrial partnership) is replicated in every architecture and design school worldwide. Its aesthetic -- minimal, functional, industrially produced -- defines the modern built environment. When the Nazis closed the school in 1933, its diaspora (Gropius and Breuer to Harvard, Mies to IIT, Moholy-Nagy to Chicago, Albers to Black Mountain and Yale) transplanted Bauhaus principles into American education, shaping postwar modernism globally.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:350:**Canonical buildings:** Villa Savoie (Le Corbusier, 1931), Barcelona Pavilion (Mies, 1929), Lever House (SOM, 1952), Seagram Building (Mies, 1958), United Nations Headquarters (Harrison et al., 1952).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:351:**Design rules:** Three principles codified by Hitchcock and Johnson: (1) architecture as volume -- thin planes enclosing space rather than mass; (2) regularity rather than axial symmetry as the ordering principle; (3) the proscription of arbitrary applied decoration. Structural grid expressed through modular repetition; glass curtain wall as primary facade technology; pilotis as standard ground-level treatment; flat roof without cornice or parapet expression; white or neutral-colored surfaces.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:352:**Legacy:** The International Style became the default language of postwar corporate, institutional, and governmental architecture worldwide. Its universalism was both its strength (adaptable, scalable, industrializable) and its weakness (accused of placelessness and cultural imperialism, provoking the postmodern reaction). Corporate modernism (SOM's Lever House and Inland Steel, Bunshaft's Beinecke Library) demonstrated that the style could serve institutional power as effectively as social idealism.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:359:**Design principles:** Wright's "grammar" of organic architecture: (1) a building should grow naturally from its site as a plant grows from the soil; (2) materials should be used in their nature -- wood as wood, stone as stone; (3) the plan should radiate outward from a central hearth/core; (4) interior and exterior spaces should flow continuously; (5) the horizontal line expresses the earth, the vertical line the spirit; (6) decoration should be integral to structure, not applied. Scharoun's "urban landscapes" treat each building as a topographic event.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:360:**Legacy:** Organic architecture provides a counternarrative to rationalist modernism, insisting that buildings emerge from particular conditions rather than universal principles. Its emphasis on site-specificity and natural process directly informs contemporary biophilic, biomimetic, and parametric design practices. Wright's influence extends to digital design through his principle of geometric grammar -- a formal system of rules generating infinite variations from a finite vocabulary, prefiguring algorithmic design.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:365:**Characteristics:** Exposed raw concrete (*beton brut*) with formwork imprints visible; massive sculptural forms; expression of mechanical services; "as found" material honesty; heroic structural spans and cantilevers; complex interlocking sections; repetitive modular units aggregated into megastructures; social idealism (public housing, civic institutions, universities).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:367:**Design principles:** "As found" material honesty -- every material visible in its raw state, including formwork impressions, aggregate exposure, and service conduits; heroic structural expression; complex interlocking sections creating spatial drama; repetitive modular units aggregated into larger configurations; integration of landscape through elevated platforms and ground-level porosity.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:368:**Legacy:** Brutalism produced the most ambitious social-housing and civic-infrastructure projects of the postwar era. After decades of disdain, it has been critically rehabilitated as an architecture of genuine social commitment and spatial power. Its influence persists in contemporary raw-concrete practices (Ando, Zumthor, Siza). The SOS Brutalism movement (2017) catalogued over 2,000 buildings worldwide and galvanized preservation efforts.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:376:**Legacy:** Metabolism's capsule-and-megastructure thinking anticipated modular construction, prefabrication, and the adaptable-infrastructure concepts now central to resilient urban design. Its utopian ambition and willingness to rethink urban form at systemic scale remain inspiring. Nakagin Capsule Tower's 2022 demolition (capsules were never actually replaced) offers a cautionary lesson about the gap between theoretical replaceability and practical maintenance.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:383:**Design principles:** Van Eyck's "twin phenomena" -- large and small, inside and outside, open and closed, individual and collective -- should be reconciled in every design decision, not resolved by choosing one over the other. Habraken's "support and infill" framework separates the permanent collective structure (supports -- load-bearing, circulation, services) from the adaptable individual dwelling (infill -- partitions, finishes, fixtures). Architecture should create "occasions" -- spatial conditions inviting unprogrammed human encounter.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:385:**Legacy:** Dutch Structuralism directly informs contemporary participatory design, open-building systems, and the mat-building typology. Hertzberger's concept of "polyvalence" -- designing forms that invite multiple interpretations and uses -- is increasingly relevant to adaptable, resilient architecture. The open-building movement (Habraken's successors) has been adopted in Japan (KSI system) and is gaining traction in Europe as regulatory frameworks for long-life buildings emerge.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:392:**Design rules:** "Double coding" -- the building must communicate simultaneously to architects (through formal and historical literacy) and to the general public (through recognizable symbols, color, and narrative). Historical quotation should be knowing, ironic, or transformative -- never literal reproduction. Context takes priority over abstract composition: street lines, cornice heights, material palettes, and local typologies should be engaged. Ornament is permitted -- indeed encouraged -- but must carry meaning beyond pure decoration.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:393:**Legacy:** Postmodernism reopened architecture to history, symbolism, and popular culture after modernism's restrictive purism. Its critical insights about communication, context, and meaning remain relevant even as its formal language has fallen from fashion. The decorated shed/duck distinction is an enduring analytical tool. "New Classicism" (Quinlan Terry, Robert A.M. Stern, Leon Krier) and "New Urbanism" (Andres Duany, Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk) are its most commercially successful legacies.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:398:**Characteristics:** Celebration of structural and mechanical systems as expressive architecture; exposed steel and tensile structures; industrial components and prefabrication; glass and transparency; flexible interior space freed by externalized services; environmental engineering (natural ventilation, solar control, green energy); technology as aesthetic and ethical commitment.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:400:**Design principles:** Structure, services, and circulation are not concealed but expressed and celebrated -- painted, exposed, articulated on the exterior. Internal space is freed for maximum flexibility by pushing permanent elements to the perimeter or exterior. Industrial components and connections are detailed with machine precision. Glass and transparency create visual connection between interior and urban context. Environmental performance (natural ventilation, solar shading, daylight) achieved through engineered systems rather than traditional devices. Color coding distinguishes building systems (blue = air, green = water, yellow = electrical, red = circulation at Pompidou).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:401:**Legacy:** High-Tech demonstrated that advanced engineering and environmental performance could produce architecture of great expressive power. It evolved into the sustainability-driven "eco-tech" of Foster, Piano, and their successors, making it arguably the most commercially successful architectural movement of the late 20th century. Santiago Calatrava extended its structural expressionism into bridge and station design.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:404:**Core text:** Jacques Derrida's philosophical writings (adapted to architecture); Mark Wigley and Philip Johnson curated the 1988 MoMA exhibition *Deconstructivist Architecture*.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:406:**Characteristics:** Fragmentation, distortion, and dislocation of architectural conventions; non-rectilinear geometries (acute angles, torqued planes, colliding volumes); challenging structural logic and perceptual stability; exposed conflict rather than resolved harmony; architecture as critical practice interrogating its own assumptions; digital design tools enabling complex curved and faceted surfaces.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:408:**Design principles:** Seven "deconstructivist architects" identified by the 1988 MoMA exhibition: Gehry, Libeskind, Koolhaas, Hadid, Eisenman, Tschumi, Coop Himmelb(l)au. Their shared formal vocabulary included: distorted grids, torqued planes, acute angles, colliding volumes, leaning walls, fractured surfaces. Philosophical underpinning from Derrida: structures of meaning (and architectural structures) contain internal contradictions that can be exposed and exploited rather than resolved. Architecture should make viewers uncomfortable with their assumptions about enclosure, gravity, order, and stability. The movement proved that buildings could be formally radical and still function.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:409:**Legacy:** Deconstructivism liberated architectural form from orthogonal convention and made digital design tools essential to practice. Its formal inventiveness directly enabled parametricism, while its critical questioning of architectural norms continues to influence academic and avant-garde practice. The 1988 show remains the most influential architecture exhibition since the 1932 International Style exhibition.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:417:**Legacy:** Critical Regionalism provides the most intellectually rigorous framework for architecture that is simultaneously modern and locally grounded. In an era of globalization and climate crisis, its insistence on topographic, climatic, and tectonic specificity is more relevant than ever. It directly informs the work of Kere, Wang Shu, Vo Trong Nghia, and every practice working with local materials in global dialogue.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:433:**Legacy:** Parametricism has massively expanded architecture's formal vocabulary and its fabrication toolkit. Critics argue it prioritizes novelty over inhabitation, but its computational methods -- generative algorithms, environmental simulation, robotic fabrication -- are now embedded in mainstream practice regardless of stylistic affiliation. Post-parametric practice increasingly uses these tools for performance optimization (structural, environmental, acoustic) rather than formal expression.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:440:**The 14 Patterns (Terrapin Bright Green, 2014):** (1) Visual connection with nature; (2) Non-visual connection with nature (sound, touch, scent); (3) Non-rhythmic sensory stimuli; (4) Thermal and airflow variability; (5) Presence of water; (6) Dynamic and diffuse light; (7) Connection with natural systems (seasonal awareness); (8) Biomorphic forms and patterns; (9) Material connection with nature; (10) Complexity and order (fractal geometry); (11) Prospect (expansive views); (12) Refuge (enclosed, protective spaces); (13) Mystery (partially obscured views inviting exploration); (14) Risk/peril (manageable sense of danger, e.g., cantilevered balcony, glass floor).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:512:| *De Re Aedificatoria* | Alberti | 1452 | Concinnitas; architect as intellectual author |
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:524:| *The Eyes of the Skin* | Pallasmaa | 1996 | Haptic architecture; multi-sensory design |
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:526:| *Yes is More* | Ingels | 2009 | Pragmatic utopianism; diagrammatic architecture |
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:535:Thermal mass (Barragan, Kere), courtyard typology (Islamic tradition), narrow streets for shade, wind towers, thick walls with small apertures, earth construction, night-sky radiative cooling. Key references: Barragan, Hassan Fathy (Egyptian, earth architecture), Neutra (desert modernism), Bawa (tropical courtyard adaptation).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:564:**1950s:** Beton brut (Le Corbusier Unite), served/servant (Kahn), shell structures (Nervi, Candela, Utzon), curtain-wall towers (Lever House, Seagram), Team X critique of CIAM.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:572:**1990s:** Digital turn (Gehry's CATIA adoption for Bilbao), blob architecture (Greg Lynn), parametric scripting (early Grasshopper precursors), LEED certification (1998), diagrid structures (Foster's Swiss Re), mass customization.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:585:Felix Candela (1910-1997) -- hyperbolic paraboloid shells of extraordinary thinness (40mm) spanning 30m+ at Xochimilco Restaurant (1958) and Bacardi Factory (1960). Heinz Isler (1926-2009) -- experimentally form-found shells using inflated membranes and frozen fabric models; Deitingen Service Station (1968) shell canopy. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:591:Shigeru Ban -- Centre Pompidou-Metz (2010) woven-glulam lattice roof; Tamedia Office Zurich (2013) all-timber seven-story structure with no metal fasteners. .\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\theorists-and-movements.md:667:**Christopher Alexander** (1936-2022): *A Pattern Language* (1977) catalogued 253 design patterns from regional scale to construction detail. *The Timeless Way of Building* (1979) theorized "the quality without a name." *The Nature of Order* (2002-2005) proposed 15 fundamental properties of living structure. His work bridges architecture, urban design, and software engineering (he directly influenced software design patterns).
