.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:3:> Dimensions, metrics, adjacencies, and exemplars for every major building type.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:40:**Critical adjacencies:** Street entry at grade > stair hall > upper bedrooms; rear garden accessible from kitchen/dining at grade or half-level; party walls continuous for acoustic separation (STC 55+).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:41:**Section strategies:** Split-level (skip-stop) for sloped sites; maisonette over flat; live-work with ground-floor commercial.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:73:**Section strategies:** Skip-stop corridors (every 3rd floor) for efficiency; setback upper floors for terraces and contextual massing; podium base with tower above for density-with-streetwall.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:85:**Parking ratio:** 0.3-1.0 spaces/unit (underground, often 2-3 below-grade levels).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:88:**Critical adjacencies:** Ground-floor lobby (double-height, 5-6m clear) > concierge/mail > elevator bank; sky lobbies at transfer floors; amenity floors (pool, gym, lounge) at podium top or upper floors for views; MEP floors every 20-25 stories; fire-refuge floors per code.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:111:**Unit size:** 12-25 m2 (micro-studio); 18-30 m2 (studio with kitchenette); cluster flats with 4-8 bedrooms sharing kitchen/living.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:117:**Critical adjacencies:** Entry/reception with parcel storage > elevator/stair core > residential floors; common rooms (lounge, study, kitchen) distributed every 2-3 floors; bicycle storage at grade; refuse centralized at grade.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:130:**Key metrics:** Corridor width 2.0-2.4m (handrails both sides); max travel distance to nurse station 30m (memory care), 60m (assisted); common dining 1.5-2.0 m2 per resident; outdoor garden 3-5 m2 per resident; nurse call in every unit and bathroom.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:132:**Exemplars:** De Hogeweyk (Molenaar & Bol & van Dillen, Netherlands, 2009 -- dementia village); Humanitas Deventer (Netherlands -- intergenerational student-senior housing); Heald Farm Court (Pozzoni, UK, 2015 -- extra-care community).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:178:**FAR:** 0.3-0.8 (suburban, single-level with parking); 1.5-4.0 (urban multi-level).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:181:**Critical adjacencies:** Anchor stores at termini of mall axes (generating pedestrian flow between them); food court at central node or upper level; cinema/entertainment at upper level (destination driver); service/loading ring around perimeter, never crossing public circulation; vertical circulation (escalators + elevators) at 60-80m intervals.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:193:**Key metrics:** Shopfront glazing: 70-90% transparency at ground level; threshold depth 0.5-1.5m (recessed entry); service access from rear lane or basement; live load 5.0-7.5 kN/m2; signage zone 0.6-1.2m above shopfront; column-free width minimum 4m.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:205:**NTG ratio:** 60-72% (high proportion of shared amenity, event, and service space).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:206:**Key metrics:** Density 4-8 m2 NIA per person (hot-desk); private offices 6-15 m2 (1-4 person); meeting rooms 1 per 15-25 members; phone booths 1 per 10-15 members; event space 50-200 m2; kitchen/cafe 1.5-2.5 m2 per 10 members; 30-40% of floor as collaboration/lounge; acoustic separation STC 40+ between offices.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:207:**Critical adjacencies:** Reception/community manager at entry > lounge/cafe zone > open co-working desks > enclosed offices along perimeter or core > meeting rooms clustered near vertical circulation > phone booths distributed throughout > event space near entry with after-hours access.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:223:**Critical adjacencies:** Admin/reception at main entry with visual control; early years clustered at ground level with direct garden access; science/art/technology in dedicated zone with shared prep; gymnasium near outdoor fields with external event access; cafeteria adjacent to kitchen and outdoor eating; library at heart of school as learning commons.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:261:**Key spatial requirements:** Climate control: 21+/-1C, 50+/-5% RH (loan-standard, ASHRAE Class AA); lighting: 50 lux (works on paper), 150-200 lux (paintings), 300 lux (sculpture); UV <75 microwatts/lumen; art handling: freight elevator 3m x 4m x 3.5m clear; loading dock with air-lock chamber for climate-controlled truck unloading; crate storage 500-2,000 m2; conservation workshop 100-400 m2.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:275:**Key spatial requirements:** Quiet reading zones with acoustic separation (NC 30-35); collaborative zones (NC 40-45) with flexible furniture; digital/media lab with AV equipment; children's area (public libraries) with lower shelving (1.2m max), soft floor, acoustic buffer; special collections with climate control (18C, 45% RH); staff processing/cataloging 80-200 m2; auditorium/event space 100-300 seats near entry.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:288:**Key spatial requirements:** Acoustic isolation from external noise (NC 15-20 for concert hall); room-within-room construction (isolated inner shell on neoprene pads); variable acoustics (retractable curtains, adjustable ceiling panels, reverberation chambers); 3-5 rehearsal rooms (1 full-size, 100-300 m2); 15-30 dressing rooms (10-15 m2 each); green room 40-80 m2; instrument storage 50-200 m2; scene shop 300-800 m2 with truck-height door; costume workshop 80-200 m2.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\architect-foundations\references\building-typology-taxonomy.md:289:**Critical adjacencies:** Public: forecourt > foyer/box office > coat check > auditorium (multiple entry vomitories); foyer with bar/interval circulation (0.5 m2 per seat); performer: stage door > sign-in > dressing rooms > green room > stage (performers and public never cross paths); scene dock directly to stage at truck-bed height (1.2m); rehearsal rooms near stage with independent access.

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:5:  impact), room acoustics and reverberation control, environmental noise
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:15:Sound is mechanical energy propagated as pressure waves through air, solids, and liquids. Architectural acoustics splits into two complementary domains: **sound insulation** (preventing unwanted sound transmission between spaces) and **room acoustics** (controlling how sound behaves within a space). Every building design decision — from structural material to partition detailing to room volume — has acoustic consequences.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:23:**Flanking transmission** is indirect sound transmission via paths other than the direct separating element. A high-performance party wall is worthless if sound bypasses it through a continuous floor slab, a shared window reveal, a back-to-back electrical socket, or a common ceiling void. In lightweight construction (steel frame, timber frame), flanking paths routinely limit achieved performance to 5–10 dB below the laboratory rating of the separating element.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:33:**Weighted Normalized Impact Sound Pressure Level (Ln,w)** — ISO equivalent of IIC, per ISO 10140-3 and ISO 717-2. Unlike IIC, lower Ln,w is better (it measures sound level received below the floor). Approximate relationship: IIC ≈ 110 - Ln,w.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:37:**Reverberation Time (RT60 or T60)** — Time in seconds for sound to decay by 60 dB after the source stops. The fundamental descriptor of a room's acoustic character. Measured per ISO 3382-1 (performance spaces) or ISO 3382-2 (ordinary rooms). Typically reported as a mid-frequency average (500/1000 Hz). Longer RT60 = more reverberant, more enveloping, less speech clarity.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:39:**Speech Transmission Index (STI)** — Measure of speech intelligibility from 0 (unintelligible) to 1 (perfect). Accounts for reverberation and background noise. Targets: STI ≥ 0.60 for classrooms (good), ≥ 0.50 for open-plan offices (fair), ≥ 0.50 for PA systems in transport hubs.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:57:The following targets represent minimum acceptable performance. Good practice exceeds these by 3–5 dB, and premium developments by 8–10 dB.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:88:**Mass law:** For a single-leaf partition, sound reduction index increases by approximately 6 dB per doubling of surface mass (kg/m²) and 6 dB per doubling of frequency. A 100 mm dense concrete wall (~240 kg/m²) achieves approximately Rw 50 dB. Doubling to 200 mm (~480 kg/m²) yields approximately Rw 56 dB.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:96:**Masonry/concrete cavity walls** — Two leaves of blockwork or concrete with a 50–100 mm cavity fully filled with mineral wool, no rigid ties. Achieves Rw 55–65 dB depending on leaf mass. Used for party walls between dwellings.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:98:**Metal stud partitions** — Single frame: 2 layers 15 mm gypsum board each side on 70 mm C-studs at 600 mm centres, 50 mm mineral wool in cavity. Achieves STC 50–55 / Rw 50–53 dB. Double frame (two independent stud rows, 25 mm gap): 2 layers gypsum board each side, mineral wool full fill. Achieves STC 60–65 / Rw 58–63 dB.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:102:**Floating floors** — Concrete screed (65–75 mm) on a resilient layer (mineral wool, rubber, closed-cell foam) placed over the structural slab. The resilient layer must turn up at edges and be isolated from walls with a perimeter strip. Achieves Rw improvement of 5–10 dB airborne and IIC improvement of 20–30 dB.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:104:**Independent ceilings** — Ceiling on separate joists or hangers not rigidly connected to the floor above. The air gap and absorption in the ceiling void provide additional insulation. Achieves 10–15 dB improvement. Used below noisy spaces (plant rooms, dance studios) or above sensitive spaces (recording studios, concert halls).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:108:**Soft floor coverings:** Carpet with underlay can improve IIC by 20–30 dB on a bare concrete slab. However, carpet cannot be guaranteed to remain for the building's life and is not accepted as the sole impact insulation strategy in most standards.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:110:**Floating screed floors:** 65 mm sand-cement screed on 25 mm resilient mineral wool (dynamic stiffness s' ≤ 20 MN/m³) over 150 mm concrete slab. Achieves Ln,w ≤ 48 dB (IIC ≥ 62). The lower the dynamic stiffness of the resilient layer, the better the impact isolation.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:112:**Timber floating floors:** 18 mm chipboard or plywood on 25 mm resilient rubber pads or cradles, over structural timber or concrete floor. Less mass than concrete screed but suitable for lightweight construction. Achieves Ln,w ≤ 53–58 dB.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:118:In completed buildings, the achieved sound insulation between rooms is the combination of the direct path (through the separating element) and all flanking paths. Flanking paths include:
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:133:5. Stagger electrical sockets by 200 mm minimum; never back-to-back in party walls

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:142:Reverberation time is the single most important descriptor of a room's acoustic character. Correct RT60 ensures speech intelligibility in communication spaces, musical richness in performance spaces, and comfort in everyday environments.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:149:| Courtroom | 0.6–0.9 s | Speech clarity, authority |

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:208:**Coupled volumes** — Two or more connected spaces with different absorption characteristics create variable acoustics. Sound decays quickly in the more absorptive space (benefiting clarity) but late energy returns from the reverberant coupled space (benefiting envelopment). Used in concert halls (reverberant chambers coupled via adjustable openings) and worship spaces.

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:228:### 4.2 Internal Noise Level Targets
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:248:**Required Rw (facade) = External noise level − Internal target + 10 dB (safety margin)**
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:271:- **Acoustic ventilators:** Through-wall or through-window units with internal sound-attenuating baffles. Achieve Dn,e,w 30–42 dB while providing trickle ventilation (typically 5–10 l/s). Types: louvered acoustic vents, acoustic trickle vents with mineral wool lining, mechanically assisted acoustic vents.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:272:- **Attenuated air paths:** Purpose-designed ventilation openings with extended acoustic path length (typically 0.5–1.0 m), lined with absorptive material. Can be integrated into facade reveals or window heads.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:308:- **Spring mounts:** Steel coil springs provide 90–98% isolation efficiency at operating speed. Static deflection 25–50 mm typical. Used for large fans, chillers, pumps. Must include a neoprene acoustic pad beneath the spring to prevent high-frequency short-circuiting.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:311:- **Flexible connections:** All pipes, ducts, and cables connecting to isolated equipment must incorporate flexible sections to prevent vibration bypass. Rubber bellows on pipes, canvas or neoprene flexible duct sections, flexible conduit for cables.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:313:**Isolation efficiency:** η = 1 − 1/(f/f₀)² for frequencies well above the natural frequency f₀. For 90% isolation, the operating frequency must be ≥3× the natural frequency of the mount. A fan at 25 Hz on springs with f₀ = 3 Hz achieves η = 99%.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:317:**Fan noise** is the primary noise source in HVAC systems. Fan sound power level increases with pressure rise and airflow volume. Backward-curved centrifugal fans are quieter than forward-curved at the same duty. Sound power: Lw = 10 + 10 log₁₀(Q) + 20 log₁₀(P) where Q is flow (m³/s) and P is total pressure (Pa). The spectrum shape depends on fan type and blade-pass frequency.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:324:- **Acoustic transfer (crosstalk):** Sound transmitted between rooms via shared ductwork. Prevent with lined duct runs of sufficient length between branches, or with duct-mounted crosstalk attenuators.

.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:399:**Reverberation time measurement** — ISO 3382-2 (ordinary rooms). Measured in unoccupied, furnished condition. Impulse source (starter pistol, balloon burst, or dodecahedral loudspeaker with MLS/sweep excitation) and omnidirectional microphone at multiple positions.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:401:**Background noise measurement** — All mechanical systems operating at typical load. NR/NC determined from octave-band sound pressure levels at representative positions.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:403:**Environmental noise measurement** — Facade sound insulation: ISO 16283-3 (loudspeaker method or traffic noise method). Verification that internal noise levels meet planning condition targets.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:417:BB93 (UK) and ANSI S12.60 (US) govern school acoustics. Classroom RT60 ≤ 0.6 s (furnished, unoccupied) is mandatory — this typically requires an acoustic ceiling tile (NRC ≥ 0.85) across 80–100% of the ceiling area plus absorption on the upper rear wall. Ambient noise target: 35 dB LAeq in teaching spaces (BB93 indoor ambient noise levels table). STC 50 between classrooms. Music rooms require STC 60+ separation from adjacent teaching spaces, with isolated floating floors and independent ceilings. Open-plan teaching areas require spatial sound decay rate D2,S ≥ 7 dB and speech privacy measures. Sports halls need RT60 ≤ 1.5 s with robust, impact-resistant acoustic panels.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:425:BCO (British Council for Offices) Guide to Specification defines office acoustic criteria. Open-plan offices: RT60 0.5–0.8 s, spatial decay D2,S ≥ 7 dB (achieved through high-NRC ceiling tiles, absorbent screens between workstations, and carpet). Background noise NR 35–40 (some masking is beneficial in open plan — too quiet and speech from colleagues is more distracting). Cellular offices: STC 45 between adjacent offices, STC 50 to boardrooms. Meeting rooms: NR 30, STC 50 from adjacent spaces, RT60 0.4–0.7 s. Teleconference/video conference rooms: lower RT60 (0.3–0.5 s) to avoid remote-end echo and ensure speech clarity for distant participants.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:433:Concert halls require the most sophisticated acoustic design of any building type. Volume per seat (8–11 m³), room shape (shoebox, vineyard, or hybrid), early reflection patterns, reverberation time (1.8–2.2 s for orchestral), stage acoustics (ensemble hearing, ST1 = −12 to −14 dB), and background noise (NR 20 maximum) must all be optimized simultaneously. The room is the instrument — every surface contributes to the acoustic character. Theatres require lower RT60 (0.7–1.0 s for drama, 1.0–1.4 s for musical theatre) to support unamplified speech. Cinemas require very low RT60 (0.4–0.6 s) and extraordinary inter-auditorium insulation (STC 65+ between adjacent auditoria to prevent low-frequency bleed from action films).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:437:Worship acoustics vary dramatically with liturgical tradition. Reverberant traditions (Catholic, Anglican, Orthodox) benefit from long RT60 (2.0–4.0 s) that supports choral music, organ, and a sense of transcendence — but at the cost of speech clarity. Speech-focused traditions (evangelical, reformed) require shorter RT60 (0.8–1.2 s) for sermon intelligibility, often with sound reinforcement. Multi-use worship spaces may employ variable acoustics (motorized curtains, rotating wall panels, coupled volumes) to serve both modes. Bell towers and organ installations require vibration isolation from the main worship space to prevent structural transmission of very high sound levels.
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:443:### 7.9 Mixed-Use Developments

If unavoidable, provide exceptional floor/ceiling insulation (STC 65+, IIC 65+) with structural isolation (floating floor + independent ceiling + structural break).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:451:- **Operational management:** Acoustic conditions should be specified in commercial leases (maximum noise levels at the boundary with residential, hours of operation, requirement for limiter on PA systems).
.\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\SKILL.md:461:**Floating floor overlays:** Thin resilient mat (5–10 mm) with overlay board (18 mm plywood or acoustic flooring system). .\shared\skills\skills-architects\acoustic-design\references\room-acoustics.md:134:**Ray tracing** models sound as rays emitted from a source, reflecting specularly off surfaces according to angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Each ray carries energy that is reduced at each reflection by the absorption coefficient of the surface. The model tracks rays until their energy falls below a threshold. Provides impulse response, RT60, early reflection patterns, and sound pressure level distribution.

.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:15:  - [2. Intent-revealing names](#2-intent-revealing-names)
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:48:The API must expose capabilities, not internal state or storage models. Never leak implementation details, such as database schemas or specific algorithms, through the interface. This encapsulation ensures that the internal architecture can be refactored or completely replaced without breaking consumers.
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:52:Prefer explicit parameter passing and dependency injection over stateful global state, singletons, registries, or environment variables for API configuration. Implicit configurations obscure dependencies from caller visibility, prevent static type safety, and introduce global state mutations that make concurrent execution and parallel testing difficult. Programmatic instantiations are statically verifiable, isolate test cases, and make dependency compilation boundaries transparent to bundling tools.
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:62:### 2. Intent-revealing names
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:64:Names should describe business intent rather than technical mechanics. For example, a method named `publishArticle()` is superior to `updateRowStatus()`. Use specific, self-descriptive terminology, like `temperatureCelsius` instead of `temp`, to prevent ambiguity and reduce reliance on external documentation.
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:68:Clearly distinguish between operations that retrieve data (queries) and operations that modify state (commands). Queries should ideally be safe and side-effect-free, allowing consumers to call them repeatedly without risk. Avoid mixing data retrieval with state mutation in a single operation, as it leads to unpredictable system behavior.
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:72:Design small, independent primitives that can be composed to create complex behaviors, rather than creating rigid, complex operations for every specific scenario. Changing one independent parameter should not have unexpected side effects on unrelated parts of the request.
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:80:In a distributed system, network failures are inevitable. Operations that change state must be designed to be idempotent, meaning they can be safely retried multiple times without producing cumulative side effects, such as double-charging. This is often achieved by requiring clients to provide a unique idempotency key or transaction identifier.
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:88:If a dependency or subsystem is failing, stop calling it immediately to prevent cascading failures. The interface should fail fast and return a specific error rather than hanging indefinitely. This preserves system resources and provides immediate feedback to the consumer.
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:100:Never return unbounded lists of data. For large datasets, prefer cursor-based (keyset) pagination over offset-based pagination. Cursors, which point to a specific record, provide constant-time performance (O(1)) and data stability. In contrast, offsets degrade in performance (O(n)) and suffer from skipped or duplicate records when data is modified during iteration.
.\shared\skills\agent-plugins\.agents\agents\reidbaker-agent\skills\api-review\references\canonical_api_design.md:108:Enforce constraints at the boundary. Use strong types, such as enums instead of raw strings, or distinct types for monetary values, to make invalid states unrepresentable.
